title: Customer Churn Analysis Report
executive_summary: Analysis of 749 customers reveals an overall churn rate of 37.7%. Monthly-contract customers churn at more than double the rate of annual-contract customers, and a high-risk segment of 100 customers with poor satisfaction and frequent support contacts churns at 71%. Premium-plan customers generate nearly 4× the lifetime value of Basic customers, making retention of that segment especially valuable.

key_findings.statement: The cleaned dataset contains 749 customers. Overall, 37.7% have churned, and the average monthly fee is $42.11.
Churn rates differ modestly across plans: Basic is highest at 38.9%, followed by Standard at 36.7%, and Premium at 36.6%. The spread between Basic and Premium is approximately 2.3 percentage points.
Churn rates by signup cohort are broadly similar across years. The 2024 cohort is highest at 39.8%, followed by 2021 at 38.0%, 2023 at 37.1%, and 2022 at 36.7%. No strong monotonic trend is evident.

Contract type is a strong churn driver. Monthly-contract customers churn at 48.3% versus 21.9% for annual-contract customers — monthly churn is 121% higher than annual, representing an increase in relative risk.
100 customers meet the at-risk criteria (≥5 support tickets and satisfaction score ≤2). This segment churns at 71.0%, nearly double the overall rate, and warrants immediate intervention.

Customer tenure averages 20.8 months (median 19.0 months, SD 13.2 months), indicating a wide spread. Mean satisfaction score is 3.42 out of 5 across the 722 customers with a non-missing score; 27 customers have no satisfaction record.

Lifetime value rises sharply with plan tier: Basic averages $463, Standard $869, and Premium $1,817. Premium LTV is 292% higher than Basic, making Premium customer retention the highest-value retention opportunity.

limitations: Satisfaction scores are missing for 27 customers (3.6%), which may introduce slight bias in satisfaction-based analyses and at-risk segment sizing.
Cohort churn rates for 2024 may be understated if some 2024 sign-ups have had insufficient time to churn, making year-over-year cohort comparisons potentially misleading.
The analysis is based on a single snapshot; without longitudinal tracking, causal relationships (e.g., whether low satisfaction drives churn or vice versa) cannot be established.
Lifetime value is computed as a mean per plan without controlling for tenure or contract type, so plan-level LTV differences may partly reflect those confounders.
conclusion: The most actionable findings are the contract-type gap (monthly customers churn 121% more than annual) and the at-risk segment (71% churn rate among 100 high-ticket, low-satisfaction customers). Prioritising annual-contract conversion and targeted outreach to the at-risk segment could meaningfully reduce churn. Given Premium customers deliver 292% more lifetime value than Basic, protecting Premium retention should be a top strategic priority.
